item.title: When Information Becomes Mental Exhaustion: God’s Invitation to Rest
item.description:
When you wake up and check your phone before your feet hit the floor, your brain has already sprinted into the day. Notifications, emails, and breaking news flood your mind before you have even had time to get ready for the day. This leaves you tired and mentally exhausted before the day truly begins.

Constant information is normal in our world today. But this does not make it healthy. We were not designed to take in all the information at our fingertips. This leads to a constant state of mental exhaustion, and this can affect our joy, relationships, and our walk with God.

What is mental exhaustion?

Mental exhaustion is not just feeling a little bit tired. It is a state of deep cognitive and emotional fatigue stemming from prolonged stress and overstimulation. Some of the most common signs of mental exhaustion include:

  • Difficulty concentrating
  • Feeling emotionally numb
  • Struggling to make decisions
  • Increased anxiety or irritability
  • Trouble resting
  • Feeling disconnected from God, self, and others

When we are faced with constant input, such as news, social media, and text messages, our brains remain in a state of constant alert. Over time, this can result in chronic mental exhaustion, which directly impacts our mental health.

How Constant Information Input Fuels Mental Exhaustion

Our brains were not designed to process thousands of pieces of information every day. When we do not disconnect from this constant information, we are subject to various effects on our minds and mental health.

The brain stays in an always-on mode Every notification, headline, and message is a demand on your attention. Your brain treats these as micro-stressors because the content is most often either urgent, emotional, or negative.

Over time, this low-level stress can lead to difficulty relaxing, heightened anxiety, and chronic mental fatigue. We are reminded in Scripture that we are not meant to live in constant alarm, but peace is hard to experience when our minds never shut down.

Attention becomes fragmented Endless scrolling and rapid content consumption teach our brains to expect constant novelty. This results in us living in fragments, such as skimming instead of deeply reading, half-listening, and being distracted while praying. When we become this fragmented, our mental exhaustion is amplified as we try to hold onto too many pieces of information at once.

Emotional overload and numbness Each day, we are exposed to grief, outrage, disaster, rage, and comparison. The input we see is other people’s successes and highlight reels, the global crisis and tragedies, or public arguments and controversies. Each of these is more than what the human heart was designed to carry.

We are not expected to carry the emotional weight of the whole world. It ends up becoming too much for us to hold onto unless we give it to God. We either feel overwhelmed or shut down emotionally, and each of these results from mental exhaustion.

The Spiritual Dimension of Mental Exhaustion

Mental exhaustion is not just a psychological issue. It also has a spiritual dimension. When the noise is constant, we have a harder time hearing God’s voice, remembering His promises, being still, and discerning what truly matters. Scripture calls us to a different place and posture.

The Invitation of Jesus to the Exhausted: Jesus speaks directly to the weary when he tells us to come to him and that he will give us rest (Matthew 11:28-30). He doesn’t say to come to Him when life is quiet. He invites us in, already burdened, tired, and overloaded. This is a promise of rest for our souls that is not found on a screen.

God’s Design for Stillness: We are called to intentional stillness in a world of nonstop input. This is not just a physical stillness. It is a mental and spiritual stillness mentioned in Psalm 46:10. It is a choice to step away from noise and resentment, recognizing that God is God and we are not.

How Mental Exhaustion Affects Mental Health

Constant information doesn’t just make us tired; it also makes us feel anxious. It also contributes to broader mental health challenges. Continuous exposure to news and arguments can trigger chronic worrying and nervousness, leading to a more intense struggle with anxiety.

This mental exhaustion leads to hopelessness or disconnection, which aligns with the symptoms of depression. Late-night scrolling before bed makes it harder to fall asleep and stay asleep, which leads to even more exhaustion. The combination of responsibilities and constant digital input increases the risk of burnout.

Mental health struggles are complex and have many causes, but reducing constant input is a meaningful and often necessary step toward healing and overcoming mental exhaustion.

A Biblical Perspective on Limits and Rest

God built limits and rhythms of rest into human life from the beginning. If He modeled it, then we must understand that observing limits is not a weakness; it is wisdom. When we ignore our limits and push through serious mental exhaustion, this is not faithfulness. We are trying to be our own source and Savior.

When constant input results in an increase in anxiety, God invites us to do more than cope. He expects us to bring to Him our burdened minds and hearts. This includes the weight of everything we have consumed, such as news, conversations, pressures, and fears.

We cannot guard our minds on our own. If we choose to focus on God’s word, we find that His peace is how our minds are truly guarded. It doesn’t mean we’re ignoring the world’s pain or injustice, but it does lead us to understand that constant negativity and noise aren’t what we are meant to dwell on daily. We get to decide.

Practical Steps to Reduce Constant Input

The goal is not to escape the world, but to live wisely within it. There are some practical, grace-filled steps we can take to shift away from constant input and ease mental exhaustion.

Identify your sources of overload When you honestly identify what is feeding your mental exhaustion, you can see that it is not random and that it has patterns and inputs that can be changed. Ask yourself if you can do without so much social media, news, messages, or podcasts. Find and remove specific accounts or chat threads that leave you drained each day.

Create gentle boundaries around technology Consider making small, deliberate changes that can serve as boundaries to protect your mind from constant intrusion. Set specific times to check the news or social media, turn off non-essential notifications, and place your phone out of reach on the side of your bed at night.

Practice daily moments of digital sabbath Just because you cannot disappear for a weekend does not mean you cannot carve out consistent breaks. Make time throughout the day to get away from the constant source of input. Quiet time in the morning, a short walk without headphones, or a few minutes of breathing and prayer in between tasks can help you reset and create a digital Sabbath that helps your mental health.

Rebuild your thought life with Scripture We can change the type of input that we receive. This means we can choose to read God’s word throughout the day instead of using digital input. It can be a short passage or a simple verse. The goal is to reflect on phrases that will cause you to hear the voice of God’s truth in overcoming mental exhaustion.

Invite community and professional help We were never designed to carry burdens alone. Talking honestly with a trusted friend or mentor when symptoms of anxiety, depression, or burnout are intense is not a lack of faith. Choosing to connect with a Christian counselor is a sign of spiritual and mental wisdom that will help you understand God-given limits and navigate toward healing.

Overcoming Mental Exhaustion

We may not be able to completely escape constant information. But we do not have to live in its grip every day. We can take small steps to limit constant information and replace it with truth, to experience something the world cannot offer: a quiet mind and a steady heart, with a soul learning to rest. It is normal to feel like change is hard and almost impossible. What makes it possible is consistency, with one little step at a time to advance toward change.

Connecting with a local Christian counselor is one way to get started on learning how to reset your mind in a restless world. If you would like more information on this process or to set up an appointment, reach out to our office or browse our online counselor directory. You can find a Christian counselor who can help you on your pathway to overcoming mental exhaustion in a noisy world.

The post When Information Becomes Mental Exhaustion: God’s Invitation to Rest appeared first on Bothell Christian Counseling.

item.title: When Every Day Feels Like Trauma
item.description:
When you think about trauma, it’s usually framed as an isolated event. Something that has happened to you that has caused a great deal of havoc on your emotions and on other parts of your life. But for some people, trauma isn’t isolated to a singular event or something easily pinpointed. Some people feel like they’re going through trauma every day, which can make ordinary experiences feel dangerous and overwhelming.

Understanding Chronic Trauma

Chronic trauma is something experts call complex trauma or C-PTSD, and it’s more common than you might think. It stems from prolonged, repeated, or inescapable traumatic events. It’s seen in cases of ongoing abuse or neglect, particularly in childhood. The intense feelings you get when you are going through trauma stretch beyond a singular event to affect core emotional regulation, relationships, sense of self, and even bodily functions.

Here’s the part that often surprises people, at least those who aren’t experiencing it. Not everyone who feels constantly on edge has experienced abuse, neglect, or any clearly identifiable traumatic event. Sometimes trauma-like feelings don’t come from a singular trauma at all. It comes simply from living in a world that can be unnervingly unpredictable, relentlessly demanding, and downright exhausting.

Causes of Chronic Trauma That Aren’t Related to a Single Trauma

There are several ways that you can develop chronic trauma symptoms that aren’t directly related to a singular traumatic event.

Your childhood environment contributes to how you process the world around you as an adult. If you grow up in a household that demands perfection, has high expectations, or doles out subtle criticism, your nervous system learns to stay alert.

Through experience, you have learned to always anticipate what’s next or what could go wrong as a protective shield against negative consequences. This learned nervous system response will continue into adulthood and will manifest as perfectionism or overwork.

Chronic stress in adulthood can have a similar effect on your nervous system. Long-term financial struggles, high-pressure jobs, caregiving responsibilities, or even living in a community where safety is uncertain can all contribute. These stressors train your body to stay in a state of high alert. While these stressors aren’t as definable as a catastrophic ordeal, they can make daily life feel like a test of endurance. Triggers that seem harmless to most can send you reeling.

Even experiences that feel normal on the surface, such as balancing school, work, and family, can contribute to this state. When life demands more than the energy you have, your nervous system can mistake these chronic pressures for real threats. This creates a loop of hypervigilance, shaping the way that you respond to situations emotionally, physically, and even spiritually.

Feeling Unsafe

One of the hardest parts of living with chronic stress or trauma-like symptoms is the disconnect between your reality and your internal perception. While you may not be in any actual danger, your mind and body perceive your circumstances as potentially harmful.

This disparity is often what puzzles the people in your life and can make your reactions to normal stressors seem like an overreach. On the outside, things might appear stable. You have a job, a home, and supportive people in your life. You may even have a faith that you hold dear. Yet, inside your body, hidden behind that confident smile, your body feels unsettled, guarded, and tense, as if danger is imminent.

This internal (and what seems like eternal) sense of unsafety can be confusing and even discouraging. But it’s important to realize that while your brain may be capable of logical thought, your nervous system isn’t.

Your nervous system doesn’t measure safety through a logical method but relies on experience to gauge danger. If your body has learned that pressure, responsibility, or unpredictability are constant, it may struggle to relax even when the present moment poses no threat.

Responding, Not Reacting

When your nervous system is stuck in survival mode, reactions tend to come faster than reason. You might find yourself snapping at people, emotionally shutting down, overthinking, or withdrawing before you even realize what’s happening. These reactions are protective and are your body’s attempt to keep you safe based on past patterns, not necessarily present-day reality.

To fully overcome your trauma symptoms, you must move away from reaction and into thoughtful and deliberate positive responses. One healthy response comes through self-awareness. Instead of judging yourself harshly for your reactionary tendencies, reframe your response to ask yourself what it is that your body is trying to protect itself from. What is the perceived danger?

While it might seem obvious to you when you slow down your body and mind, the perceived threat might not always be at the forefront of your mind while you’re experiencing your trauma responses. Over time, you’ll begin to see exactly what you’re fearing or feeling threatened by. And when you understand what the threat is, you can work toward neutralizing the threat and overcoming your fear.

This mental reframing will also shift you from self-criticism to curiosity. You can shift ideas like I’m so out of control or “I am always so nervous because I’m always in danger to mere curiosity.” Instead, you could reframe it to “Why am I always nervous when there’s no immediate threat?”

God of Peace

Isn’t it wonderful to know that the God of all Creation, the Prince of Peace Himself, is an active, loving Father who wants to interact with you? It’s comforting to remember that God sees every moment in your life, even the ones where you’re weary and struggling with hidden pain, even when others overlook the pressure you feel because it’s not like traditional trauma.

When you pause and reframe before you react, you open a place where God can meet you. Matthew 11:28-30 extends a beautiful invitation to us. It tells us to come to Jesus when we are burdened. To come to Him when we are weary. And He will give us rest. What an awesome gift rest is to those who have hypervigilance or chronic stress.

When you’re burdened, turn to Him. A quick prayer or a spontaneous song of worship can make a big difference in how you feel. Not only are you inviting the creator of peace into your stress, but you are unloading your burden straight onto His loving and broad shoulders.

Therapy can help

Many people who feel chronic stress but who haven’t had an obvious trauma shy away from therapy. They hesitate to seek help because they believe their stress doesn’t qualify them for professional therapy. They believe that because their trauma experience isn’t clearly defined, they aren’t actually victims of its snares.

But therapy isn’t reserved for worst-case scenarios. It’s a private, safe space where you can start to understand why your body and mind are responding to everyday life in the way they are. You can explore how to interrupt the default emotion of stress in non-threatening situations.

Understanding your chronic stress is the first step toward healing. Your hypervigilance is a signal of perceived danger. It acts as a sign that it’s time to slow down and listen to what your nervous system has been trying to tell you.

If you’re living in survival mode and have been for a long time, learning how to rest can feel uncomfortable and unfamiliar at first. Feeling safe can be relearned. As your body and mind learn how to respond to triggers and stress predictably and healthily, you will start to respond neutrally to things and situations that trigger you now.

This is your invitation and permission to pay attention to your mind and body. Take one intentional step toward stripping away the unexplained trauma in your life. Call our offices to set an appointment with a counselor. A therapist can help you understand your trauma and responses and give you tools that can help you live a fuller, more peaceful life.

The post When Every Day Feels Like Trauma appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: New Women’s Insecurities Brought About by the Digital Era
item.description:
As long as we can remember, women have had to face insurmountable hurdles and overcome great impediments that have contributed to women’s insecurities for centuries.

Women across the world have had to fight for basic human rights such as voting, owning property, and walking without an escort. Sadly, some of our fellow women are still fighting for these rights in other parts of the world to this day.

However, the 21st century has generally brought about a significant reduction in some of these practices against women. Many traditional practices and beliefs that traditionally contributed to women’s insecurities, like gender bias, workplace inequalities, gender-based violence, and social stigmas, were issues modern women thought were behind us.

But just when women had begun to walk in light of this progress, a new and unexpected challenge has emerged, reviving women’s struggles with insecurities yet again.

The Rise of the Digital Era

The digital era, also known as the Digital Revolution or Information Age, began in the mid-twentieth century. It has been marked by the transition from traditional industries to an economy centered on information technology. This has had a profound impact on women, bringing both opportunities and challenges.

Opportunities the digital world has opened for women include:

Economic Empowerment Digital technologies have opened new job opportunities, particularly in tech and remote work, allowing women to balance work and family responsibilities more effectively.

Education and Skills Development Online learning platforms have made education more accessible, enabling women to acquire new skills and advance their careers.

Entrepreneurship The internet has provided a platform for women entrepreneurs to start and grow businesses, reaching global markets with minimal investment.

Advocacy and Activism Social media and digital tools have empowered women to advocate for their rights, raise awareness about gender issues, and mobilize support for social causes.

While the opportunities are immense, the tech era has also introduced new insecurities for women, impacting various aspects of their lives. From biased algorithms to enhanced cybersecurity threats and everything in between, this whole new era is piling on a new set of pressure for women than ever before.

Unexpected Tech-Related Concerns that are Increasing Women’s Insecurities

AI and Algorithm Biases There is already evidence that many of the AI technologies and algorithms being developed can perpetuate gender bias and negative stereotyping. When this technology is applied to hiring processes, women have unfortunately fallen short.

Some studies have shown that job hiring algorithms favor men for technical roles while steering women toward positions requiring skills that are typically lower paid. These job imbalances can make women undervalued or unfairly judged based on biased data.

The Imposter Phenomenon A feeling of not belonging is a common experience for women when it comes to the tech industry. It has been exacerbated by the industry’s gender imbalance, the fast-paced nature of the tech industry, and the high visibility of male tech achievements while female achievements are suppressed.

For example, the gross underrepresentation in tech leadership roles has left many feeling like they aren’t as adequate or competent as their peers in tech.

Rise of Cybersecurity Threats Statistically, women have been targeted more aggressively in cyberattacks such as deepfakes, doxxing, and online harassment. Women who experience online humiliation and cyberbullying can have a pervasive sense of insecurity and fear about their online presence and suffer significant emotional distress, anxiety, and even PTSD.

How Tech-Related Insecurities in Women Manifest

  • Body Image Issues
  • Increased Privacy Concerns
  • Social Isolation
  • Overcompensation
  • Self-Doubt
  • Reluctance to Speak Up

The prevalence of social media platforms has amplified unrealistic beauty standards. Women often feel pressured to conform to these ideals, leading to issues like body dysmorphia, low self-esteem, vulnerability, and fear. To counteract their insecurities, some women may overcompensate by working excessively hard, striving for perfection, or taking on more responsibilities than necessary.

Women in tech may also frequently question their skills and knowledge, feeling as if they aren’t as competent as their male counterparts. This often leads to reluctance to take on challenging projects or apply for leadership roles.

The digital age has blurred the lines between work and personal life, making it challenging for women to maintain a healthy work-life balance, resulting in increased stress and burnout.

All these new women’s insecurities in the digital world highlight the need for greater understanding, dialogue, and resources to help women navigate the digital landscape confidently and safely. There is a need for more inclusive practices and support systems in the tech industry to help women feel secure and valued.

Possible Strategies for Women to Overcome Tech-Based Insecurities

Maintaining work-life balance in the digital age can be challenging, but there are several effective strategies to help manage. Setting clear boundaries, like specific work hours, ensures that everyone in your life knows and respects your personal time.

Other ways to help navigate the complexities of the digital age while maintaining a healthy work-life balance include:

  • Prioritizing ourselves and making time for activities that promote our well-being, such as exercise, cherished hobbies, and relaxation. Regular breaks and physical activity can help mitigate the effects of digital overload.
  • Negotiating flexible work arrangements that suit us as women and mothers and can allow a balance between work and personal commitments. Demanding validation of our unique needs as women, such as flexible hours or remote work options, is not a sign of weakness but rather empowerment.
  • Learning how to use technology mindfully by leveraging productivity tools to manage our time effectively and eliminate the potential for digital distractions. A good tip is to set specific times to check messages, emails, and social pages to avoid constant interruptions.
  • Scheduling regular times for digital detox is crucial to help us as women unwind and unplug from social and work-related technology. This can help to recharge and maintain a healthy balance between being always on and having personal peace of mind.
  • Being realistic and practical about what we can achieve in a day and avoiding overcommitting does not make us less of a woman but rather promotes our wholeness. We don’t have to be “Wonder Woman,” and it’s okay to say no when necessary to prevent burnout and to accept that we don’t have to do extra to prove our worth.

Understanding and addressing these new digital-related issues that are increasing women’s insecurities requires a multifaceted approach, including promoting digital literacy, creating supportive online communities, and advocating for more inclusive practices in tech industries.

As a woman in this fast-paced digital landscape, it’s okay to admit that you need to seek support to get over any hurts and insecurities that you feel. Overcoming tech-related insecurities can be challenging, but professional help can make a significant difference.

Here are some options to consider:

  • A career coach who specializes in tech can provide guidance on career development, skill enhancement, and overcoming workplace challenges.
  • A mentor you can find in your field can provide invaluable support and advice. Mentors share their experiences, offer guidance, and can help you navigate the complexities of the tech industry.
  • An occasional professional development workshop or training session, focused on building technical skills and soft skills, can boost your confidence. Such programs often include networking opportunities, which can also help reduce feelings of isolation.
  • A support group for women in tech can provide a sense of community and shared understanding. Support groups offer emotional support, practical advice, and a platform to share experiences.
  • An online program to bolster your skills on various tech topics is a great morale booster. Enhancing your skills through these courses can help you feel more competent and confident in your abilities.
  • A mindfulness activity like meditation, yoga, or stress management techniques can help you manage anxiety and build resilience.
  • A therapist or counselor can help you explore the root causes of your insecurities, develop strategies to build confidence, and address negative thought patterns.

Women’s insecurities about tech-related matters are more common than any of us may believe, but nothing to be ashamed of.

If you have more questions or would like to talk to a professional about which of these options is best suited for you, you can find specific resources or professionals right here on this website. Call the numbers you see here today.

The post New Women’s Insecurities Brought About by the Digital Era appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: What is Depression? A Christian Counselor in Spokane, WA Explains
item.description:
I have worked with many clients who suffer from depression too, and I found myself always needing more information about what exactly depression is. I have known family members who have struggled with it, as well as friends and colleagues over the years.

So, I determined to take a medium dive into the literature to see if I could feel at the end of that journey that I could put my arms around what depression is, what its causes are, and what some viable treatments are. This is the first of three parts that cover the subject.

As I began to read from several academically reviewed sources, the journey did not really land on solid ground. I still feel that depression is like this fog or mist from a Stephen King novel that covers everything and that we don’t know about it. It lurks out there as an invisible impending threat.

We have all been through times when we felt emotionally down without explanation or that things were so stressful that we felt destined to fail at whatever challenge was ahead. Or, as life can be, we have been dealt some serious losses.

Freud said that depression (he called it melancholia) “is an affective disorder characterized by a deeply painful mood, a loss of interest in the outside world, a loss of ability to love, the inhibition of every achievement and the lowering of self-esteem, which manifests itself in self-reproach and self-abuse” (Leuzinger-Bohleber et. al. p. 1). Sounds familiar, doesn’t it?

Essentially, depression is a persistent low mood that affects most areas of one’s life and shapes the way one interprets the world in which they live. Depression is a serious mental illness, and it is not a sign of a weakling state or some character flaw. In ancient civilizations, the common view of depression was that people who were depressed for extended periods had spiritual problems.

The Greeks thought that causeless depression was due to internal body fluids like bile. In the 18th and 19th centuries, these ideas persisted, and some other theories emerged, but the treatment of these folks was horrific. Such things as being locked into asylums, bloodletting, immersion into water for as long as one could stand, and spinning stools, to name a few.

In the 19th and 20th centuries, such ideas as electroshock and lobotomies were introduced. I mention this past to put into perspective where we are today. We have a greater understanding of the ramifications or symptoms of depression, as well as having made much progress in treatments.

Prevalence

If misery loves company, then there is a lot of company among the depressed in our modern world. As of September 2025, the percentage of adults who reported being depressed in their lifetime at least once was 28.5%. For adolescents and young adults, the prevalence was almost 20%, and 8.3% had had at least one major depressive episode. There is consistent research over the past several decades that females are more likely than males to have depression.

For the elderly, the numbers are difficult to assess and are likely undiagnosed because people tend to think their symptoms are normal for their age. One report found that almost 50% of older folks in nursing homes displayed depressive symptoms. I suspect this phenomenon with the elderly speaks to some of our societal flaws. About 36% of depressed elderly folks receive any treatment for their condition and are less likely to receive treatment as they get older.

From my days as a Marriage and Family Therapy graduate student, I focused on the elderly and discovered the suicide rate for that group is high and likely way underreported. This is likely due to not knowing if an overdose of meds was intentional or not. And shockingly, most completed suicides were with firearms.

Major Depressive Disorder and its qualifying symptoms serve as a marker for gathering data on the prevalence of depression among groups of people. Though many people can experience a single episode, there is consistent research that shows that most people who have one episode are 50-80% more likely to have another episode in their life.

Teens are vulnerable to depression. There are many reasons for this, but it seems obvious that social media immersion has contributed to the greater occurrence. About 18% of adolescents aged 12-17 have had a major depressive episode.

Adolescents are keenly aware of their standing in their world and are often hypersensitive – they always have been. What’s more important than being cool? It doesn’t take much to send a teen down the rabbit hole of insecurity of their self.

The sadness that comes from depression is most often rooted in a negative self-evaluation. No doubt, certain circumstances in life can get one down. Financial stress, unemployment, death of a loved one, or any misfortune outside of oneself can easily be turned inward. These troubles become difficult to process, and though they seem to come from outside yourself, you reason that an internal flaw can better explain the troubles.

“In depression, what feels lost or damaged is part of oneself” (McWilliam, p 234). Common statements by the depressed have been “I’m not good enough, I’m flawed, I’m self-indulgent, I’m evil” (p. 235).

The poor soul is driven to take an inward look and doesn’t like what he/she sees. “Depressive people are agonizingly aware of every sin they have committed, every kindness they have neglected to extend, every selfish inclination that has crossed their minds.” (p. 239).

The sources of these thoughts are legion. They are often a result of how they have perceived others’ responses to them, often from an early age. The seed of self-doubt and self-disappointment or loathing often comes from the adults in their lives who sent that message or valued peers who seem to hold a grip over their sense of self-worth.

Some inexplicable sources for depression could connect to biology/genetics or a combination of factors. We will delve into this in part two of this series.

Symptoms

Before I share the clinical diagnostic symptoms for depression, it’s important to know that several physical symptoms can be attributed to depression. Depression affects the body. Many folks experience unexplained aches and pains in the muscles or joints. If there is a chronic pain issue, it could get worse. Many have complained of back pain or headaches.

Perpetual fatigue is common even when getting enough sleep. Sleep is often disturbed by either insomnia or hypersomnia. While depressed, there is often the experience of eating binges and gaining weight, and conversely, loss of appetite and significant weight loss. Gastrointestinal issues are also common.

There are often changes in one’s physical movement, being either slowed down or agitated. In addition to these marked symptoms is a reduction in sexual drive. The point is that depression adversely affects the whole person, not just the mind.

The DSM 5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders) is the common tool to determine a given mental disorder. The keyword is “disorder.” To qualify, the disturbance needs to negatively impact one or more aspects of one’s life. The description of the disorder makes no statement of judgment, does not imply cause, nor does it offer treatment. The following is word for word from the of the DSM 5 regarding Major Depressive Disorder (MDD).

1. Five (or more) of the following symptoms have been present during the same week period and represent a change from previous functioning; at least one of the symptoms is (1) depressed mood or (2) loss of interest or pleasure.

2. Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, as indicated by either subjective report (e.g., feels sad, empty, hopeless) or observation made by others (note: in children and adolescents, can be irritable mood.

3. Markedly diminished interest in pleasure in all, or almost all, activities most of the day, nearly every day (as indicated by either subjective account or observation)

4. Significant weight loss when not dieting or weight gain (e.g., a change of more than 5% of body weight in a month) or decrease or increase in appetite nearly every day.

5. Insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day.

6. Psychomotor agitation or retardation nearly every day (observable by others, not merely subjective feeling or restlessness or being slowed down).

7. Fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day

8. Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt (which may be delusional) nearly every day (not merely self-reproach or guilt about being sick).

9. Diminished ability to concentrate, or indecisiveness, nearly every day (either by subjective account or as observed by others).

10. Recurrent thoughts of death (not just fear of dying), recurrent suicidal ideation without a specific plan, or a suicide attempt or a specific plan for committing suicide.

11. The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

12. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or other medical condition.

American Psychiatric Association. (2022). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed., text rev.). https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.books.9780890425787 [1]

There is another diagnostic resource known as the International Classification System for Diseases (ICD) that mirrors most of the symptom criteria that is in the DSM 5. Specifically, the diagnostic code is ICD-10 for major depressive disorder.

Depression can be a persistent condition as well. In major depressive disorder, the condition can come and then leave for a time or never come back. But Persistent Depressive Disorder, sometimes referred to as dysthymia, is a condition that lasts two years or more. The criteria for PDD are much like MDD. One of the characteristics is that it is resistant to treatment and is considered a more severe condition.

The symptoms of these illnesses are serious and should not be ignored by the one experiencing them or those who might witness them. Depression is not a condition in which you can just exhort the person to snap out of it, pull themselves up, or tell them to think differently.

There are several theories about the causes of this illness, but it should not be treated any differently than if someone has diabetes or a heart condition or any other disease where we don’t judge the character of someone for having it.

The symptoms can be on a spectrum of mild to severe, so keep that in mind as you consider how you are feeling or as you consider someone else. If you or someone you care about is experiencing these symptoms as listed above. Please feel free to contact me at 509-569-7102 or email me at martyr@spokaneschristiancounseling.com.

If you feel your safety or the safety of someone you care about is in jeopardy, please call 988 or 911 immediately to get appropriate help.

item.title: PTSD and Relationships: How You Can Find Hope by Healing Together
item.description:
Trauma doesn’t stay contained to one person. PTSD and relationships are often intertwined because of the effects of post-traumatic stress. This ripples out and touches the people closest to you. Partners, friends, and family members often navigate the unfamiliar territory of emotional distance and protective walls within these relationships. The person they love has built barriers that feel impossible to cross because of trauma.

This isn’t about understanding what PTSD is. The challenge involves recognizing how the trauma will reshape how you connect, trust, and feel safe with others around you. The result is complex, where the survivor and their loved ones try to bridge a gap.

Both people involved may feel stuck, unsure of how to help each other without making things worse. There is hope when both people are willing to walk toward healing and restoration, instead of surviving the trauma.

When Trauma Changes How Someone Connects

PTSD can alter the way a person experiences a relationship. The brain’s response to trauma has created a pattern of hypervigilance, emotional numbing, and avoidance that was not there before. Some may retreat into silence, while others may pull away from physical touch. These changes aren’t character flaws or choices; they are survival mechanisms. The brain developed an automatic survival response to protect itself from perceived danger.

When the survivor’s protective response clashes with the partner’s need for connection, there’s a difficult balance that has emerged. One person is trying to feel safe by creating distance, and the other is feeling abandoned and confused because of the withdrawal. Both people are hurting, and neither one is wrong. The result becomes a cycle in which one person seeks more connection, and the other withdraws more, leaving the relationship feeling as though it’s unraveling.

There are times when both people blame themselves, which makes the situation more painful. The survivor feels guilty for not being able to get over it, and the partner wonders what they did wrong. PTSD isn’t about blame, it is about a brain that has been rewired by trauma and needs compassionate support to find long-term healing. Recognizing this distinction is often the first step toward finding a way forward together.

It’s always good to remember God’s promises about healing. In Psalm 147, we are reminded how He handles our broken, wounded places: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” (Psalm 147:3, NIV)

The Hidden Impact on Partners and Loved Ones

Most of the attention focuses on the person with PTSD, which can leave their loved ones experiencing their own form of trauma. Secondary traumatic stress is real, and when families absorb the emotional weight of someone else’s pain, it can take a toll. These family members experience their own anxiety, depression, and exhaustion from constantly managing a crisis.

Christian counselors can provide crucial support for both individuals. This form of counseling helps partners understand that caring for themselves doesn’t diminish their commitment to their loved one. A partner who is emotionally healthy and spiritually grounded is far better equipped to offer steady, compassionate support over long-term healing.

The capacity to be present over the long haul is strengthened as they find that setting boundaries, expressing needs, and seeking support are acts of wisdom, not selfishness. It is how they can follow the guidance in Galatians: “Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.” (Galatians 6:2, NIV)

Rebuilding Trust When PTSD and Relationships Collide

One of the first struggles of PTSD and relationships is trust. Trauma has taught the brain that the world is dangerous and people cannot be trusted. Even though a partner has done nothing to warrant distrust, the survivor’s nervous system remains on high alert and interprets neutral actions as threats. A delayed text response may begin to register as evidence of abandonment. Anger or rejection can be read into certain tones in the other person’s voice.

Rebuilding trust requires patience that often feels unimaginable. It involves the partners consistently showing up, remaining steady, and not taking the distrust personally, even when it hurts. The survivor is required to work on recognizing when their trauma responses are distorting reality. This isn’t a quick process, and there will be setbacks, but progress is possible when both people are committed to the healing process.

Christian counselors are trained to help couples develop practical strategies for trust building. These strategies include creating predictable routines to help the survivor feel safe and practicing transparent communication to reduce misunderstandings. In some cases, it may require establishing check-in rituals that ensure connection without becoming codependent. Small, consistent actions are the foundations that will enable trust to grow again.

Communication Strategies that Honor Both Hearts

When PTSD and relationships collide, communication is often the first thing to break down. The survivor faces challenges articulating what they are feeling or needing, especially during heightened emotional flooding or a flashback. The partners ask questions or offer solutions that may feel invasive or dismissive, even though they are only trying to help. Each person ends up frustrated and more disconnected.

Effective communication and trauma recovery start with recognizing that a survivor in a triggered state cannot engage in rational conversation. These moments require grounding and safety instead of resolution. Partners must learn to offer a calm presence rather than trying to fix the problem.

Finding a rhythm for communication works best when it happens outside of the hard moments. Couples can carve out intentional times to talk through difficult topics or lean on written communication when face-to-face conversations feel like too much.

Christian counselors guide couples in finding the approaches that work for their unique dynamic. This creates a communication style that honors both individuals, where trauma survivors find safety and partners feel heard.

There are also opportunities for deeper spiritual connections that result from navigating these conversations. Praying as a couple and acknowledging dependence on God’s guidance becomes a shared practice that quietly strengthens the relationship over time. Scripture reading offers wisdom that reminds them both that they are not alone in their challenges.

Hope for Healing Together

Even though PTSD creates real challenges in a relationship, it does not have to be the end of connection and intimacy. When the survivor and their loved one approach healing with honesty, patience, and professional support, these relationships can deepen and strengthen beyond simply surviving. This journey isn’t linear, and there will be difficult days, but each small step forward and each moment of vulnerability can build toward lasting hope.

Faith offers a foundation that will sustain a couple through this process. When both people acknowledge they are not alone, that God is present in their healing, and that healing is possible through His grace, they find the strength needed to persevere through this healing journey.

Christian counselors integrate the spiritual dimension and evidence-based trauma treatment to address the psychological and spiritual aspects of recovery such as Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR), Somatic Experiencing, and/or Internal Family System (IFS). This combination addresses not just the symptoms of trauma but the deeper wounds that affect how a person relates to God, to themselves, and to the people they love.

This builds hope that something new can emerge, rather than simply returning to what existed before the trauma. Healing for this couple won’t happen in isolation. It requires that they reach out for help and choose courage over fear one day at a time.

If PTSD is affecting your relationship, you do not have to navigate this journey alone. You can contact our office and connect with experienced Christian counselors who understand trauma recovery and relationship healing.

Photo:
“White Flower”, Courtesy of Ayana Bula, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Pink Flower”, Courtesy of Mourad Saadi, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

Read more at PTSD and Relationships: How You Can Find Hope by Healing Together | Everett Christian Counseling.

A delayed text response may begin to register as evidence of abandonment. Anger or rejection can be read into certain tones in the other person’s voice.

Rebuilding trust requires patience that often feels unimaginable. It involves the partners consistently showing up, remaining steady, and not taking the distrust personally, even when it hurts. The survivor is required to work on recognizing when their trauma responses are distorting reality. This isn’t a quick process, and there will be setbacks, but progress is possible when both people are committed to the healing process.

Christian counselors are trained to help couples develop practical strategies for trust building. These strategies include creating predictable routines to help the survivor feel safe and practicing transparent communication to reduce misunderstandings. In some cases, it may require establishing check-in rituals that ensure connection without becoming codependent. Small, consistent actions are the foundations that will enable trust to grow again.

Communication Strategies that Honor Both Hearts

When PTSD and relationships collide, communication is often the first thing to break down. The survivor faces challenges articulating what they are feeling or needing, especially during heightened emotional flooding or a flashback. The partners ask questions or offer solutions that may feel invasive or dismissive, even though they are only trying to help. Each person ends up frustrated and more disconnected.

Effective communication and trauma recovery start with recognizing that a survivor in a triggered state cannot engage in rational conversation. These moments require grounding and safety instead of resolution. Partners must learn to offer a calm presence rather than trying to fix the problem.

Finding a rhythm for communication works best when it happens outside of the hard moments. Couples can carve out intentional times to talk through difficult topics or lean on written communication when face-to-face conversations feel like too much.

Christian counselors guide couples in finding the approaches that work for their unique dynamic. This creates a communication style that honors both individuals, where trauma survivors find safety and partners feel heard.

There are also opportunities for deeper spiritual connections that result from navigating these conversations. Praying as a couple and acknowledging dependence on God’s guidance becomes a shared practice that quietly strengthens the relationship over time. Scripture reading offers wisdom that reminds them both that they are not alone in their challenges.

Hope for Healing Together

Even though PTSD creates real challenges in a relationship, it does not have to be the end of connection and intimacy. When the survivor and their loved one approach healing with honesty, patience, and professional support, these relationships can deepen and strengthen beyond simply surviving. This journey isn’t linear, and there will be difficult days, but each small step forward and each moment of vulnerability can build toward lasting hope.

Faith offers a foundation that will sustain a couple through this process. When both people acknowledge they are not alone, that God is present in their healing, and that healing is possible through His grace, they find the strength needed to persevere through this healing journey.

Christian counselors integrate the spiritual dimension and evidence-based trauma treatment to address the psychological and spiritual aspects of recovery such as Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR), Somatic Experiencing, and/or Internal Family System (IFS). This combination addresses not just the symptoms of trauma but the deeper wounds that affect how a person relates to God, to themselves, and to the people they love.

This builds hope that something new can emerge, rather than simply returning to what existed before the trauma. Healing for this couple won’t happen in isolation. It requires that they reach out for help and choose courage over fear one day at a time.

If PTSD is affecting your relationship, you do not have to navigate this journey alone. You can contact our office and connect with experienced Christian counselors who understand trauma recovery and relationship healing.

item.title: PTSD and Relationships: How You Can Find Hope by Healing Together
item.description:
Trauma doesn’t stay contained to one person. PTSD and relationships are often intertwined because of the effects of post-traumatic stress. This ripples out and touches the people closest to you. Partners, friends, and family members often navigate the unfamiliar territory of emotional distance and protective walls within these relationships. The person they love has built barriers that feel impossible to cross because of trauma.

This isn’t about understanding what PTSD is. The challenge involves recognizing how the trauma will reshape how you connect, trust, and feel safe with others around you. The result is complex, where the survivor and their loved ones try to bridge a gap.

Both people involved may feel stuck, unsure of how to help each other without making things worse. There is hope when both people are willing to walk toward healing and restoration, instead of surviving the trauma.

PTSD can alter the way a person experiences a relationship. The brain’s response to trauma has created a pattern of hypervigilance, emotional numbing, and avoidance that was not there before. Some may retreat into silence, while others may pull away from physical touch. These changes aren’t character flaws or choices; they are survival mechanisms. The brain developed an automatic survival response to protect itself from perceived danger.

When the survivor’s protective response clashes with the partner’s need for connection, there’s a difficult balance that has emerged. One person is trying to feel safe by creating distance, and the other is feeling abandoned and confused because of the withdrawal. Both people are hurting, and neither one is wrong. The result becomes a cycle in which one person seeks more connection, and the other withdraws more, leaving the relationship feeling as though it’s unraveling.

There are times when both people blame themselves, which makes the situation more painful. The survivor feels guilty for not being able to get over it, and the partner wonders what they did wrong. Recognizing this distinction is often the first step toward finding a way forward together.

It’s always good to remember God’s promises about healing. In Psalm 147, we are reminded how He handles our broken, wounded places: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” (Psalm 147:3, NIV)

Secondary traumatic stress is real, and when families absorb the emotional weight of someone else’s pain, it can take a toll. These family members experience their own anxiety, depression, and exhaustion from constantly managing a crisis.

A partner who is emotionally healthy and spiritually grounded is far better equipped to offer steady, compassionate support over long-term healing.

item.title: Divorce and Children: What Your Kids Want You to Know About Their Emotional Needs
item.description:
No one plans on getting divorced when they say, “I do.” But life happens. Previous family-of-origin cultural norms and communication styles can tend to stand at the forefront of unresolved issues. Circumstances change, and people can grow apart, with unresolved resentment and unforgiveness. When people begin to only exist in their marriage, interactions and healthy communication will become difficult, and sometimes divorce may become unavoidable.

While divorce can be a trauma for the adults going through it, it can have an even bigger impact on the children involved. Depending on the age of the child, normally they do not have the emotional vocabulary to express their discomfort watching their parents’ struggle. Interestingly, children see and feel the uneasiness parents are experiencing but are not saying. It is true, actions do speak louder than words.

What do your children want you to know as they go through this crisis with you? Right, it is not just you and your spouse who are experiencing internal turmoil. Wouldn’t it be great if you could read your children’s minds? Understand their fears?

Then you would know how to comfort them. What to say. You’d know how to reassure them and offer hope and comfort for the upcoming changes that will require a sense of safety mentally, emotionally, and physically, so that your love will remain.

Some children may be able to express their innermost thoughts and feelings, but most lack the emotional maturity, vocabulary, and self-awareness needed to communicate their emotions truly. As a parent, you may not understand why they are acting out.

Here’s what your children may want to express to you. The letters below depict what a child may think or feel during the divorce process. Read them and consider how these thoughts and feelings may relate to your child.

I’m confused

Dear Mom and Dad,

You know what’s going on between the two of you. You know how the divorce process works, but I don’t. I don’t have the life experience you do, so the only idea of what a divorce is comes from what some of my friends say at school and a few movies I’ve seen. And it hasn’t been good.

I literally don’t know what’s going on. Attorney? Custody? These are all just foreign words to me, and I have no idea what they mean or if I even need to learn them.

All I know is that it’s really bad. I thought we had a good family. I don’t know what happened. I know you were arguing, and it was loud. Mom would cry, one of you would slam a door or leave the house, but you came back. I know you have been distant from each other, but I don’t know when you stopped loving each other. And if you can stop loving each other, what would prevent you from stopping loving me?

Love,
Your Child

Divorce is confusing, even when you’re the adult going through it. This is even more true when you’re a child who is being dragged along with no vote or power into the unknown. Not only is the situation scary, but it’s uncertain. There are many unanswered questions that the child doesn’t know to ask or is afraid to ask. They may be feeling left out or abandoned.

Even the terminology that gets tossed around during divorce proceedings can be confusing for everyone except for maybe your lawyer and the judge. Unless you’ve been through it before, you’re not likely to be an expert in divorce proceedings, so imagine how disorienting this whole new, scary world is for your child, who has even less life experience.

Take the time to talk with your child about your marriage and what is happening. Kids need honesty, but they need age-appropriate honesty. Tell them that the trouble your family is facing isn’t their fault and that you’re still figuring out the details.

Give them the child-sized version of the situation. They will appreciate your honesty. It will help to orient them. It is important to inform your children before there is a court date. You may wish to seek professional help for this step.

I need stability

Dear Mom and Dad,

I know we’re going through a transition as a family; sometimes I feel like I’m lost. I love you both, but I feel guilty sometimes. Does this mean I have to choose? This sucks. Are we still family? Probably not. Sometimes I feel like I’ve been in a really bad earthquake and everything around me has fallen to the ground.

Yeah, after earthquakes, people rebuild slowly, but we are not a building; we are a family – or at least we used to be. New buildings look good, but how do you rebuild your family? What do I rebuild with? What is going to be strong enough since our family wasn’t strong enough when the earthquake hit?

With everything changing in my world, I need the tremors to stop so I can orient myself in this new life. Does this mean we have to move away from my friends, my neighborhood, or my grandparents? Please don’t make me change schools or give up my room. I need something familiar, something to hold onto when everything around me is changing.

Love,

Your Child

A change in lifestyle is practically inevitable during a divorce. Separating lives means moving into new places, changing your schedules, and editing your social circle. Just because your life is changing doesn’t mean theirs has to. It’s important not to change theirs unnecessarily. Try to maintain some semblance of normalcy for your children during this tumultuous time.

Help them maintain the good parts of their lives that they’re used to. Just because you’re angry with the in-laws doesn’t mean that you should pull your children away from the comfort of their familiarity. Just because going to a certain restaurant triggers painful memories in you doesn’t mean that you should ban your children from it.

And just because you desperately want to integrate your new love interest into your life, doesn’t mean your children are ready for it. We shouldn’t deny them the opportunity to heal. Learn to be self-aware of your internal feelings, thoughts, and reactions as well as those of your children. Each of you are experiencing grief and loss. Your grief and loss may be experienced differently, but they are experienced.

Never put your child in the position to choose sides or become a secret agent gathering information on the other parent during or after the divorce proceeding. You will be setting yourself up for more pain and discomfort.

Many parents make the unfortunate mistake of pitting their children against the other parent. It’s quite natural for humans to try to rally support in the midst of a crisis or try to convince others that their actions are justified or that they are the victim. But this is not your child’s job. Don’t make your children into soldiers, spies, or your emotional support team. They are children, and they deserve to have an uninterrupted relationship with both parents.

I need permission to express my emotions

Dear Mom and Dad,

Sometimes I feel guilty when I enjoy being with one of you. I don’t want the other person to be sad or feel left out. I don’t want to cause you more hurt. So sometimes I pretend to be less happy than I am. Sometimes I pretend to be happy when I’m not.

Please tell me it’s okay to smile, laugh, and have fun with both of you. Please tell me that loving one parent doesn’t mean that I’m betraying the other. Tell me I can cry when I feel it without upsetting you.

Love,

Your Child

Children feel responsible for protecting their parents’ feelings. They might hide joy, affection, or excitement because they think it’ll hurt the other parent. They might suppress tears so they don’t stress you out. Tell them that you’re glad when they spend time with the other parent and that you know they love you, even when they’re not with you.

Give your child permission to cry or even be angry. This allows them to be wholly invested in both parental relationships. It gives them the freedom to be authentic in their emotions and authentic with you.

Consider taking your child to a Christian therapist who will help them understand their emotions. Therapy can give them a platform to discuss how they feel without worrying about how it might affect either parent. A therapist can give them space to feel and live authentically and provide coping skills to use when things feel overwhelming.

Moving Forward

What would your child tell you as you go through a divorce? They would tell you that they want you to be happy, but they don’t want to be responsible for it. They would tell you they love you both and that they need more help than they feel they can ask for.

Divorce may change the structure of your family, but it doesn’t have to destroy your child’s life. God gave you your children as a precious gift. As their parents, it’s your job to be a good steward of that gift. Pay attention to what their actions are conveying because they don’t always have the confidence or vocabulary to verbally tell you themselves.

Help them find the help they need through therapy and reassure them that no matter what happens, God still loves them and wants to help. Put your children’s hearts first so they can emerge from the divorce with the same innocence they had before, but with more coping skills and a renewed assurance that they’re loved.

Contact our reception team today to schedule an appointment with me or one of the other Christian counselors in our online directory. You can also seek positive support through your church or Christian divorce support groups.

“Cyclist”, Courtesy of Tim Graf, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Blonde Girl”, Courtesy of Katie Gerrard, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; 

The post Divorce and Children: What Your Kids Want You to Know About Their Emotional Needs appeared first on Mill Creek Christian Counseling.

Never put your child in the position to choose sides or become a secret agent gathering information on the other parent during or after the divorce proceeding. You will be setting yourself up for more pain and discomfort.

Many parents make the unfortunate mistake of pitting their children against the other parent. It’s quite natural for humans to try to rally support in the midst of a crisis or try to convince others that their actions are justified or that they are the victim. But this is not your child’s job. Don’t make your children into soldiers, spies, or your emotional support team. They are children, and they deserve to have an uninterrupted relationship with both parents.

I need permission to express my emotions

Dear Mom and Dad,

Sometimes I feel guilty when I enjoy being with one of you. I don’t want the other person to be sad or feel left out. I don’t want to cause you more hurt. So sometimes I pretend to be less happy than I am. Sometimes I pretend to be happy when I’m not.

Please tell me it’s okay to smile, laugh, and have fun with both of you. Please tell me that loving one parent doesn’t mean that I’m betraying the other. Tell me I can cry when I feel it without upsetting you.

Love,

Your Child

They might suppress tears so they don’t stress you out. Tell them that you’re glad when they spend time with the other parent and that you know they love you, even when they’re not with you.

Give your child permission to cry or even be angry. This allows them to be wholly invested in both parental relationships. It gives them the freedom to be authentic in their emotions and authentic with you.

Consider taking your child to a Christian therapist who will help them understand their emotions. Therapy can give them a platform to discuss how they feel without worrying about how it might affect either parent. A therapist can give them space to feel and live authentically and provide coping skills to use when things feel overwhelming.

Moving Forward

What would your child tell you as you go through a divorce? They would tell you that they want you to be happy, but they don’t want to be responsible for it. They would tell you they love you both and that they need more help than they feel they can ask for.

Divorce may change the structure of your family, but it doesn’t have to destroy your child’s life. God gave you your children as a precious gift. As their parents, it’s your job to be a good steward of that gift. Pay attention to what their actions are conveying because they don’t always have the confidence or vocabulary to verbally tell you themselves.

Help them find the help they need through therapy and reassure them that no matter what happens, God still loves them and wants to help. Put your children’s hearts first so they can emerge from the divorce with the same innocence they had before, but with more coping skills and a renewed assurance that they’re loved.

Contact our reception team today to schedule an appointment with me or one of the other Christian counselors in our online directory. You can also seek positive support through your church or Christian divorce support groups.

item.title: Divorce and Children: What Your Kids Want You to Know About Their Emotional Needs
item.description:
No one plans on getting divorced when they say, “I do.” But life happens. Previous family-of-origin cultural norms and communication styles can tend to stand at the forefront of unresolved issues. Circumstances change, and people can grow apart, with unresolved resentment and unforgiveness. When people begin to only exist in their marriage, interactions and healthy communication will become difficult, and sometimes divorce may become unavoidable.

While divorce can be a trauma for the adults going through it, it can have an even bigger impact on the children involved. Depending on the age of the child, normally they do not have the emotional vocabulary to express their discomfort watching their parents’ struggle. Interestingly, children see and feel the uneasiness parents are experiencing but are not saying. It is true, actions do speak louder than words.

What do your children want you to know as they go through this crisis with you? Right, it is not just you and your spouse who are experiencing internal turmoil. Wouldn’t it be great if you could read your children’s minds? Understand their fears?

Then you would know how to comfort them. What to say. You’d know how to reassure them and offer hope and comfort for the upcoming changes that will require a sense of safety mentally, emotionally, and physically, so that your love will remain.

Some children may be able to express their innermost thoughts and feelings, but most lack the emotional maturity, vocabulary, and self-awareness needed to communicate their emotions truly. As a parent, you may not understand why they are acting out.

Here’s what your children may want to express to you. The letters below depict what a child may think or feel during the divorce process. Read them and consider how these thoughts and feelings may relate to your child.

I’m confused

Dear Mom and Dad,

You know what’s going on between the two of you. You know how the divorce process works, but I don’t. I don’t have the life experience you do, so the only idea of what a divorce is comes from what some of my friends say at school and a few movies I’ve seen. And it hasn’t been good.

I literally don’t know what’s going on. Attorney? Custody? These are all just foreign words to me, and I have no idea what they mean or if I even need to learn them.

All I know is that it’s really bad. I thought we had a good family. I don’t know what happened. I know you were arguing, and it was loud. Mom would cry, one of you would slam a door or leave the house, but you came back. I know you have been distant from each other, but I don’t know when you stopped loving each other. And if you can stop loving each other, what would prevent you from stopping loving me?

Love,
Your Child

Divorce is confusing, even when you’re the adult going through it. This is even more true when you’re a child who is being dragged along with no vote or power into the unknown. Not only is the situation scary, but it’s uncertain. There are many unanswered questions that the child doesn’t know to ask or is afraid to ask. They may be feeling left out or abandoned.

Even the terminology that gets tossed around during divorce proceedings can be confusing for everyone except for maybe your lawyer and the judge. Unless you’ve been through it before, you’re not likely to be an expert in divorce proceedings, so imagine how disorienting this whole new, scary world is for your child, who has even less life experience.

Take the time to talk with your child about your marriage and what is happening. Kids need honesty, but they need age-appropriate honesty. Tell them that the trouble your family is facing isn’t their fault and that you’re still figuring out the details.

Give them the child-sized version of the situation. They will appreciate your honesty. It will help to orient them. It is important to inform your children before there is a court date. You may wish to seek professional help for this step.

I need stability

Dear Mom and Dad,

I know we’re going through a transition as a family; sometimes I feel like I’m lost. I love you both, but I feel guilty sometimes. Does this mean I have to choose? This sucks. Are we still family? Probably not. Sometimes I feel like I’ve been in a really bad earthquake and everything around me has fallen to the ground.

Yeah, after earthquakes, people rebuild slowly, but we are not a building; we are a family – or at least we used to be. New buildings look good, but how do you rebuild your family? What do I rebuild with? What is going to be strong enough since our family wasn’t strong enough when the earthquake hit?

With everything changing in my world, I need the tremors to stop so I can orient myself in this new life. Does this mean we have to move away from my friends, my neighborhood, or my grandparents? Please don’t make me change schools or give up my room. I need something familiar, something to hold onto when everything around me is changing.

Love,

Your Child

A change in lifestyle is practically inevitable during a divorce. Separating lives means moving into new places, changing your schedules, and editing your social circle. Just because your life is changing doesn’t mean theirs has to. It’s important not to change theirs unnecessarily. Try to maintain some semblance of normalcy for your children during this tumultuous time.

Help them maintain the good parts of their lives that they’re used to. Just because you’re angry with the in-laws doesn’t mean that you should pull your children away from the comfort of their familiarity. Just because going to a certain restaurant triggers painful memories in you doesn’t mean that you should ban your children from it.

And just because you desperately want to integrate your new love interest into your life, doesn’t mean your children are ready for it. We shouldn’t deny them the opportunity to heal. Learn to be self-aware of your internal feelings, thoughts, and reactions as well as those of your children. Each of you are experiencing grief and loss. Your grief and loss may be experienced differently, but they are experienced.

Never put your child in the position to choose sides or become a secret agent gathering information on the other parent during or after the divorce proceeding. You will be setting yourself up for more pain and discomfort.

Many parents make the unfortunate mistake of pitting their children against the other parent. It’s quite natural for humans to try to rally support in the midst of a crisis or try to convince others that their actions are justified or that they are the victim. But this is not your child’s job. Don’t make your children into soldiers, spies, or your emotional support team. They are children, and they deserve to have an uninterrupted relationship with both parents.

I need permission to express my emotions

Dear Mom and Dad,

Sometimes I feel guilty when I enjoy being with one of you. I don’t want the other person to be sad or feel left out. I don’t want to cause you more hurt. So sometimes I pretend to be less happy than I am. Sometimes I pretend to be happy when I’m not.

Please tell me it’s okay to smile, laugh, and have fun with both of you. Please tell me that loving one parent doesn’t mean that I’m betraying the other. Tell me I can cry when I feel it without upsetting you.

Love,

Your Child

Children feel responsible for protecting their parents’ feelings. They might hide joy, affection, or excitement because they think it’ll hurt the other parent. They might suppress tears so they don’t stress you out. Tell them that you’re glad when they spend time with the other parent and that you know they love you, even when they’re not with you.

Give your child permission to cry or even be angry. This allows them to be wholly invested in both parental relationships. It gives them the freedom to be authentic in their emotions and authentic with you.

Consider taking your child to a Christian therapist who will help them understand their emotions. Therapy can give them a platform to discuss how they feel without worrying about how it might affect either parent. A therapist can give them space to feel and live authentically and provide coping skills to use when things feel overwhelming.

Moving Forward

What would your child tell you as you go through a divorce? They would tell you that they want you to be happy, but they don’t want to be responsible for it. They would tell you they love you both and that they need more help than they feel they can ask for.

Divorce may change the structure of your family, but it doesn’t have to destroy your child’s life. God gave you your children as a precious gift. As their parents, it’s your job to be a good steward of that gift. Pay attention to what their actions are conveying because they don’t always have the confidence or vocabulary to verbally tell you themselves.

Help them find the help they need through therapy and reassure them that no matter what happens, God still loves them and wants to help. Put your children’s hearts first so they can emerge from the divorce with the same innocence they had before, but with more coping skills and a renewed assurance that they’re loved.

Contact our reception team today to schedule an appointment with me or one of the other Christian counselors in our online directory. You can also seek positive support through your church or Christian divorce support groups.
